title: Ramadan: the whole book again
tomorrow: the last ten: why stay up for a night nobody can name?

lines: A SHEET BY THE MASJID DOOR.
cards: A sign-up sheet is taped by the masjid door. One column of names, one column of parts of the Qur'an. Somebody's aunt has claimed the long ones.
A teenager has written his name in pencil, just in case. By the month's end, between them, the whole book will have been read. That's a khatm, a completion.

But why this month? The answer is a scene in Medina, in a report kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. Every night of Ramadan, the angel Jibril comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the two of them go over the Qur'an together.
Every year. Until one year, it changes.

teach.h: THE MONTH THE BOOK CAME DOWN.
teach.b: Start with how the Qur'an names the month. In Pickthall's words: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind." The fast and the book belong together.
The month is the book's season.
Ibn 'Abbas, who tells the nightly scene, adds a detail: the Prophet was generous all year, and most generous in Ramadan, when Jibril met him, quicker to give than a blowing wind.
Reading the book and opening the hand, in the same nights. Now the change.

Another report says Jibril went over the Qur'an with him once each year, and in the year he died, twice. His daughter Fatima remembered him telling her quietly: twice this year. I think my time is near.
So the sheet by the masjid door carries an old scene inside it. Not a race to the last page.
A going-over, together, in the month the book came, the way the Prophet and Jibril did it, year after year.
One to tell a friend tonight: the last Ramadan of his life was the one where the book was read through twice.

how: In Ramadan many Muslims aim to read the whole Qur'an, alone or shared out among family or a masjid, and in some masjids the night prayers recite it through over the month.

o: the festival that ends a long season of fasting
the night the Prophet first heard a revelation
the month of fasting, when the Qur'an came down

games.q: who's who in the scene — tap the pairs.
p: a completion of the whole Qur'an
went over the Qur'an each Ramadan
heard him say: twice this year
the month the Qur'an was revealed

s: the Qur'an itself ties Ramadan to the Qur'an
2:185: the month in which the Qur'an was revealed.
a khatm only counts if one person reads it all alone
a khatm is a completion; a sheet by the door shares the parts across the month.
in a report, Jibril went over the Qur'an with the Prophet twice in his last year
and Fatima remembered him reading it as a sign his time was near.

games.q: your cousin's study group splits the Qur'an for a Ramadan khatm. she drew a long part, and finals land that week. what fits the old pattern?
o: drop out; a khatm only counts if every part is read perfectly.
keep her part and go over it with a friend, a little each night.
skim it all on the last night; finishing is the whole point.
games.why: Jibril and the Prophet went over it together, night by night, through the month. the habit is a going-over, not a sprint to the last page.

practice: Open the Qur'an, in Arabic or in a translation, to any page, or find a recitation to listen to. Read one passage aloud, slowly, as if someone were going over it beside you.
If you're keeping a khatm this year, let this be the next page of your juz'.

wordCard.voice: Ramadan: the month of fasting, which the Qur'an names as the month it was revealed. Its oldest habit is going through the book again.

orig.note: Arabic: the month of fasting, named in Qur'an 2:185 as the month the Qur'an was revealed.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the book in the month, read again because it came then. Block D keeps turning.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6 (Ibn 'Abbas: Jibril met him every night of Ramadan to study the Qur'an; most generous in Ramadan, more than the blowing wind)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4998 (Jibril reviewed the Qur'an with him once a year, twice in the year he died)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3623–3624 (Fatima: he told her Jibril reviewed it twice that year, and he took it as a sign his death was near)
